hook.text: Two lines of identical length. Add inward arrows to one and outward arrows to the other. Now one looks longer.

buildup.text: The Müller-Lyer illusion has fooled people since 1889. Even knowing it's an illusion doesn't make it disappear.

discovery.text: One theory: the arrows mimic depth cues from corners. Inward arrows look like an inside corner (closer, so seems bigger).

twist.text: But people from cultures without rectangular buildings—like the San people—are barely affected by the illusion.

climax.text: This illusion isn't hardwired. It's learned from a lifetime of processing a carpentered, right-angled environment.

punchline.text: Your illusions are shaped by the world you grew up in.

quiz.question: Why are some cultures less affected by the Müller-Lyer illusion?
options: Their environment has fewer right angles
They are trained to resist it

details.summary: The Müller-Lyer illusion makes two lines of equal length appear different because of arrowhead-like fins at their ends. Outward fins make a line look longer; inward fins make it look shorter. Despite knowing the lines are equal, the illusion persists because it operates at a low perceptual level.
details.whyItMatters: The Müller-Lyer illusion proves that knowing about an illusion does not make it disappear. Perception and knowledge operate on separate systems.
takeaways: Arrow fins change the perceived length of identical lines
The illusion persists even when you know both lines are equal
It demonstrates perception's independence from knowledge

faq.question: Why does the Müller-Lyer illusion work?
faq.answer: The leading theory is that the fin configurations mimic depth cues in the environment. Outward fins resemble the inside corner of a room, which your brain interprets as farther away and therefore larger. Inward fins resemble an outside corner, interpreted as closer and smaller.

faq.question: Does the illusion affect everyone equally?
faq.answer: No. People from cultures with fewer rectangular buildings, like the San people, are less susceptible. This supports the carpentered world hypothesis: growing up surrounded by straight walls and corners trains your visual system to interpret the fin patterns as depth cues.
